ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The aim of this paper is to elucidate the mechanisms controlling the brittle-to-ductile transition (BDT) in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline body-centred cubic (bcc) metals by the example of cold rolled tungsten (W).

For this purpose, five sheets were rolled out from one and the same sintered ingot, by various levels, representing degrees of deformation of 1.8, 2.5, 3.0, 3.4, and 4.1 (this refers to 83.5%, 91.8%, 95.0%, 96.7%, and 98.3% in the technical notation). Toughness tests show that the BDT temperature decreases with increasing degree of deformation from 115 °C ± 15 °C (388 K ± 15 K) down to −65 °C ± 15 °C (208 K ± 15 K). This is an improvement of >600 K compared with a sintered ingot.

In this paper we perform an in-depth analysis of the microstructure of the five sheets mentioned above. This analysis includes the assessment of (i) crystallographic texture, (ii) grain size and (iii) dislocation density. A comparison between microstructural features and experimental data confirms our working hypothesis which states that the BDT is controlled by the glide of screw dislocations and that the transition temperature decreases with decreasing spacing, λ, of dislocation sources along the crack front. Sources for dislocations may be the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front (BDT-temperature-grain-size-relation) or dislocation multiplication processes such as e.g., the expansion of open and closed loops (impact of dislocation density).

ce:section.ce:para: Famous failures of man-made structures put the focus on the question of why many materials exhibit a transition from brittle behaviour at low temperature to a ductile response at higher temperatures [1]. Despite great efforts made in experimental and theoretical investigations, the mechanisms controlling the brittle-to-ductile transition (BDT) remain unclear.

Tungsten (W) has been chosen as a model material to determine the mechanisms controlling the BDT in metals by many scientists [2,3]. Tungsten is almost elastically isotropic (A = 1.00641 [4]) and possesses the highest melting point among all pure metals (T
m = 3693 K [4]). It crystallizes in a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure, and thus possesses several surprising low-temperature deformation features such as (i) non-Schmid effects (tension-compression asymmetry) [5], (ii) anomalous slip (plastic slip on slip systems that do not have the highest resolved shear stress) [6–10], and (iii) the temperature and strain-rate dependence of the yield and flow stress [11,12].

The above mentioned peculiar features can at least partially be traced back to the non-planar spreading of the dislocation core of a 0/2⟨111⟩ screw dislocations (a 0 = lattice constant). Calculations confirmed that the core is extended and three-dimensional and that it has a three-fold symmetry in the absence of a stress field [13–15]. This extended dislocation core structure provides an explanation for the large Peierls stress which is overcome by thermally activated nucleation of steps on the dislocation line, known as kink pairs, and their subsequent sideward relaxation [16,17]. Giannattasio et al. [3] propose that the glide of the screw dislocations or more precisely the kink-pair nucleation process plays an important role in the mechanisms controlling the BDT in bcc metals.

The occurrence of brittle or ductile material behaviour is the result of the competition between the breaking of chemical bonds between the atoms at the crack tip and the mechanisms that govern crack tip plasticity (Fig. 1a,b) [18].

A model for crack tip plasticity was proposed by Roberts et al. [19–21] and Hartmaier et al. [22–24]. Both groups modelled crack tip plasticity by means of discrete dislocation dynamics. Their models makes use of a global, externally applied load, K
app , and a local, effective stress intensity, K
eff , at the crack tip. The effective stress intensity at the crack tip differs from the applied load, as the elastic stress fields from dislocations either increase (anti-shielding dislocations) or decrease (shielding dislocations) K
eff . The critical parameter for fracture is the Griffith critical stress intensity, K
IC , which can be determined by atomistic modelling [25]. If K
eff reaches the critical stress intensity, then fracture will occur (K
eff = K
IC ). If K
eff never reaches K
IC for any applied load, then the material shows ductile behaviour.

The nucleation of dislocations takes place in the vicinity of the crack tip where dislocations are emitted from dipole sources. Dislocations that move to the crack tip are referred to as anti-shielding dislocations. Image forces make them glide to the crack tip free surface where they are annihilated and thus cause crack tip blunting. Dislocations that glide away from the crack tip are so called shielding dislocations. They form an inverse pile up combined with a dislocation free zone between the inverse pile up and the dislocation source. The existence of a dislocation free zone and an inverse dislocation pile up was discovered by transmission election microscopy investigations by Ohr [26].

Simply said, crack tip plasticity can be described as the net result of the following sequential processes: (i) the nucleation of fresh dislocations from sources, (ii) their glide through the crystal, and (iii) their pile up at long-range obstacles such as grain boundaries. It can be anticipated that the slowest of these processes is rate controlling and thus controls the BDT. But which one is the slowest?

For single crystalline materials the BDT can either be controlled by dislocation nucleation (see process (i) in Fig. 1) or by dislocation glide (see process (ii)). Models describing the BDT as a nucleation-controlled event assume that the nucleation of fresh dislocations from sources is to slow to provide an effective shielding [18,27]. Models describing the BDT as a mobility-controlled event assume that dislocations are generated in large numbers but cannot leave the crack-tip region fast enough and thus inhibit the instantaneous nucleation of further dislocations [20,28].

For silicon, high purity, dislocation free single crystals are commercially available. This is why several groups used this material as a model material [28–32]. It was found that the activation energy of the BDT agrees well with the activation energy for dislocation mobility, ∆H
d , which can be derived from dislocation velocity measurements. Based on this results Samuels and Roberts concluded that the BDT is controlled by the glide of dislocations (see process (ii) in Fig. 1) [31]. The approach of comparing the activation energy of the BDT, ∆H
BDT , with the activation energy for dislocation mobility, ∆H
d , was also successfully applied for intrinsic silicon, n-type silicon [31], alumina [33], intrinsic germanium [34] and molybdenum [35] single crystals.

Giannattasio et al. [36] then tried to apply this working method not only for metalloids such as silicon but also for transition metals such as tungsten. Unfortunately, the data for dislocation velocity in tungsten is scarce. So Giannattasio and Roberts [37] compared the activation energy of the BDT, ∆H
BDT , with the effective kink-pair formation enthalpy, H
kp , which can be deduced from mechanical flow stress measurements combined with Seeger's theory of kink-pair formation [38]. Their experimental results gave a value of 1.00 ± 0.04 eV (W single crystal, crack system of {100}⟨001⟩, {crack plane}⟨crack front direction⟩). Furthermore, they calculated an effective kink-pair formation enthalpy, H
kp , of 1.11 eV. As both values are in a good agreement, Giannattasio and Roberts [37] conclude that the BDT in tungsten is controlled by the glide of dislocations (see process (ii) in Fig. 1) or more precisely by the glide of screw dislocations which overcome the Peierls barrier via the kink-pair nucleation process.

So the mechanisms controlling the BDT in single crystalline tungsten are well described and understood to a large extent. However, for polycrystalline tungsten, the situation is rather complex, as now the impact of grain boundaries on the BDT and the transition temperature has to be considered.

The question of the role of grain boundaries on the BDT temperature has not yet been resolved, as the role of grain boundaries is contradictory. On the one hand, grain boundaries act as obstacles for dislocation glide and can confine the plastic zone [39]. Gliding dislocations are piled up at grain boundaries and thus inhibit the instantaneous nucleation of further dislocations. Based on these considerations, a decrease of the grain size would lead to an increase of the transition temperature and the slowest process in the crack tip region may be the dislocation-grain-boundary-interaction (see process (iii) in Fig. 1). On the other hand, the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front are preferred dislocation nucleation sites. It is speculated that the transition temperature decreases with decreasing distance of the spacing of dislocation nucleation sites along the crack front, λ, i.e., with decreasing grain size [40].

It can be expected that both mechanisms (i) blocking of gliding dislocations and (ii) acting as dislocation nucleation site apply for grain boundaries. The question is just how to weight the individual contribution.

In order to elucidate the mechanisms controlling the BDT in polycrystalline tungsten, we recently produced five sheets that were rolled out from one and the same sintered ingot, by various levels, representing degrees of deformation in the range of 1.8–4.1. Toughness tests show that the BDT temperature decreases with increasing degree of deformation from 115 °C ± 15 °C (388 K ± 15 K) down to −65 °C ± 15 °C (208 K ± 15 K) [40]. This is an improvement of >600 K compared with a sintered ingot (Fig. 2a).

Based on these results, we pose the following working hypothesis for the mechanisms controlling the BDT in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline tungsten:
1.
As in single crystalline tungsten, the BDT in polycrystalline tungsten is still controlled by the glide of screw dislocations, i.e. by the kink-pair nucleation process. So the slowest process in the crack tip region is the glide of screw dislocations. This means that the activation energy of the BDT, ∆H
BDT , should be similar to the activation energy for dislocation mobility, ∆H
d (derived from dislocation velocity measurements), or the effective kink-pair formation enthalpy, H
kp (derived from Seeger's theory of kink-pair formation [38]), or the activation enthalpy for dislocation slip, ∆H
S (derived from transient mechanical tests).
2.
The temperature at which the transition occurs decreases with decreasing spacing, λ, of dislocation sources along the crack front. Sources for dislocations may be
a.
the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front or
b.
multiplication processes such as e.g. the expansion of open and closed loops, the double cross-slip mechanism [41], the triple junction mechanism [42] or others [43–45].
3.
Furthermore, the processes described above are overlapped by the geometrical arrangement of areas with high and low fracture toughness with respect to the crack system. Grain boundaries (GB) and former sinter pores (FSP) are expected to have a lower toughness compared to the grain interior: K

The aim of this paper is to provide an in-depth assessment of the microstructure of the five sheets presented above, which should then allow the answering of the following main questions:
1.
What is the impact of (i) crystallographic texture, (ii) grain size and (iii) dislocation density on the BDT temperature?
2.
Is it possible to resolve the question of the contradictory role of long-range obstacles on the BDT temperature (obstacles for dislocations glide vs. sources for dislocations)?
3.
How can a correlation between experimental data and microstructural features give indications towards a change from nucleation controlled to multiplication controlled crack tip plasticity?
4.
To what extent can the above described working hypothesis be verified or falsified?

The paper is organized as follows: First, in the “Materials and methods” section, details on the fabrication history of the five sample materials as well as the methods used to describe the crystallographic texture, grain size and dislocation density are briefly described. In particular, the results of the toughness tests, which were presented in-depth in our previous paper, are precisely recalled. In the “Results” section, the rolling induced evolution of (i) crystallographic texture, (ii) grain size, and (iii) dislocation density is shown and these microstructural features are correlated with BDT temperatures. Finally, in the “Discussion” section, our working hypothesis is verified/falsified/refined and a complete description of the BDT in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline tungsten is presented. The paper closes with a brief conclusion.

In this section, we give details on the fabrication of the materials and in particular on the rolling properties, and summarise the main outcome of the toughness test campaign. Details on the mechanical experiments can be found in Ref. [40]. Afterwards, we present the methods used to describe crystallographic texture, grain size and dislocation density.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Materials: fabrication history and mechanical properties

ce:section.ce:para: The material analysed within this paper are tungsten sheets produced by PLANSEE SE in Reutte, Austria, in a powder metallurgical process.

Five sheets were rolled out from one and the same sintered ingot. The sintered compact had a metallic purity >99.97 wt% W, a density of approximately 96% and consisted of equiaxed grains with a mean grain size of 11 μm [46].

The tungsten sintered ingot was preheated to a temperature > 1200 °C and was subsequently rolled down to a thickness of h 1 (hot rolling). Afterwards, the plate was preheated at a temperature < 1000 °C (cold rolling, CR) and was then rolled down to various extents, representing degrees of deformation of 1.8, 2.5, 3.0, and 3.4 (this refers to 83.5%, 91.8%, 95.0%, and 96.7%, in the technical notation). At each of the mentioned steps, the plate was cut and one piece was kept for further testing. In a final step, the plate was preheated at a temperature < 300 °C (low-temperature rolling, LTR) and an additional degree of deformation of 0.7 was applied. This means that the most heavily rolled tungsten sheet was deformed with an accumulative degree of cold and low-temperature rolling of 3.4 + 0.7 = 4.1 (i.e. 98.3%).
The samples were tested in their as-rolled condition, so no further stress relieve annealing was performed. The rolling was unidirectional for all the sheets.

The aim of the chemical analysis is to specify the metallic purity of the tungsten sheets and to assess whether the content of impurities increases during rolling, e.g., by wear of the rolls. Table 1 shows C, N, O, P and S, which are typical grain boundary segregation elements. Furthermore, Table 1 displays the rolling induced evolution of Cr, Mn, and Fe which are suggested to be main elements of the rolls. In total, the chemical analysis covers 19 elements. The results are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

A CS-analyser was used for the quantification of C and S, carrier gas hot extraction (CGHE) for O and N, and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) for the remaining elements.

The idea of using tungsten sheets rolled out from one and the same sintered ingot was to reduce the discussion on the mechanism controlling the BDT to the influence of the microstructure only, as the chemical composition is expected to be the same for all the sheets. This expectation is confirmed by Table 1, as the content of impurities stays almost constant during rolling. So, the contamination of the tungsten sheets during rolling is marginal and in a first approximation negligible.
The experimental setup and the results of the toughness tests were described in-depth in Ref. [40] and will thus only briefly be summarised here.

From the five as-rolled plates, single edge crack tension (SECT) samples were wire-cut by electrical discharge machining. The contour and the notch were cut; the as-rolled surface of the samples remained untouched. So, the samples had different thicknesses and the thickness of the sample is the thickness of the tungsten sheet. Roughness values of the samples' surfaces can be found in Table 2 . The samples had dimensions of 9.5 mm × 37.5 mm with a 4.75 mm-long starting crack and represent the L-T crack systems (Fig. 2b). For details on the two-letter code the reader is referred to Ref. [48].

Toughness tests were performed according to the standard ASTM E399 [48]. The criteria for brittle, semi-brittle and ductile material behaviour can be found in Ref. [40]. The loading rate was 1 MPa(m)1/2 1/s. We made use of the definition of the BDT temperature by Gumbsch [49] which says that macroscopically the transition from brittle to ductile response usually correlates with the maximum in fracture toughness. The transition temperatures are marked by vertical lines in Fig. 2a, and are summarised in Table 2.

It is well established that toughness is a function of the thickness of the sheet, viz. of the crack tip stress state in the fracture process zone (plane strain vs. plane stress dominated plastic zone) [50]. However, and this is most important for this paper, the BDT temperature is independent of the thickness of the sheet.
The crystallographic texture and grain size were determined by electron backscatter diffraction measurements; dislocation density was derived from X-ray diffraction measurements.

The investigation of the microstructure was performed using a Zeiss Merlin field-emission-gun scanning electron microscope equipped with an EDAX Hikari electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) camera. The analyses were performed using an acceleration voltage of 15 kV, 10 nA probe current and a step size of 40 nm (5 × 5 binning).
During post-processing of the EBSD data sets, pixels with a confident index <0.1 were removed. Apart from a grain confidence index standardization, no clean-up of the datasets was performed.

Crystallographic textures were determined by evaluating the EBSD data. Orientation distribution functions (ODFs) were generated by using the harmonic series expansion in the formulation of Bunge [51] to a rank of 34 and smoothed by selecting a Gaussian half-width of 5° [52].

To reduce the impact of local inhomogeneities on the texture measurements, multiple maps were recorded and stitched afterwards [53]. The result of this procedure can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 2, in which the pole figures of the five tungsten sheets are displayed. It can be seen that the pole figures are almost symmetric, which is a clear indication that the measured areas were big enough to be representative.

Grain sizes were calculated on the basis of the EBSD data and by using the line intercept method. The average intercept length of 300 lines running in the normal direction (ND), the transversal direction (TD) and the rolling direction (RD) gives the average grain size. Disorientations between 2° and 15° were considered as low angle grain boundaries, while disorientations exceeding 15° were considered as high angle grain boundaries.

The dislocation density was determined by X-ray diffraction measurements. Line profiles were recorded using a Seifert GmbH Bragg-Brentano type XRD. Cu Kα radiation was used from a tube with Cu anode operating at 40 kV and 30 mA. A Meteor 1D detector was used for recording the diffraction intensities. The scanned surface's normal pointed towards the ND. The regime between 10° and 135° (2θ) was scanned with a step size of 0.01°. The acquisition time for each step was 360 s. After the measurement, Kα2 intensities were eliminated by a Rachinger correction.

The modified Williamson-Hall method was used to calculate the dislocation densities [54]. The broadening of {110}, {200}, {211} and {310} peaks were considered in the calculations. The majority of the selected peaks possessed maximum intensities significantly above 10 k counts, which guarantees a high level of statistical reliability of the results [55]. The dimensionless factor M, characterizing the effective outer cut-off radius was assumed to be 2 [56] in the final calculations.

Here we determine the rolling induced evolution of the crystallographic texture, grain size and dislocation density and derive quantitative values for a BDT-microstructure correlation. The following three sections are organized as follows: first, an in-depth analysis of the microstructure is performed. Afterwards, the impact of selected microstructural features on the decrease of the BDT temperature is discussed.

Fig. 3 shows the orientation distribution function in the φ 2 = 45°-sections of the Euler space. It can be seen that the highest intensities are recorded along the α-fibre (fibre axis: <110> || RD; relevant components belonging to the fibre: {001} < 110>, {112} < 110>, {111} < 110>, {110} < 110>) and the γ-fibre (fibre axis: <111> || ND, relevant components: {111} < 110>, {111} < 112>). As a first approximation, it can be said that the component with the highest intensity is the {001} < 110> component, referred to as ‘rotated cube’. The maximum intensity increases from 20.4 (W1.8CR) up to 44.8 (W4.1LTR) multiple times random (m.t.r.).

An impression of the strong dominance of the texture components along the α- and γ-fibre on the overall crystallographic texture can be gained from Fig. 4 . In the diagram in Fig. 4, the number of all pixels with a certain property, divided by the number of all indexed pixels in the EBSD map (= area fraction) is plotted against the degree of deformation. It can be seen that for the most heavily cold rolled sheet, 80% of all texture components are components positioned at the α- and γ-fibre. Furthermore, the diagram in Fig. 4 shows that the area fraction of components belonging to the γ-fibre stays constant during rolling, while the area fraction of texture components of the α-fibre steadily increases. In addition, Fig. 4 displays selected microstructures shown with view in the transversal direction. Again, the rolling induced increase of the dominance of α-fibre textures (highlighted in light grey) can be anticipated. Furthermore, the position of α-fibre components with respect to γ-fibre components (dark grey) and components that do neither belong to the α- nor to the γ-fibre (white) is displayed.

By plotting the orientation density along the α- and γ-fibre, further information can be inferred (Fig. 5 ). First, it can be found that the cold rolling textures of the five tungsten sheets are to some extent similar to those of bcc metals reported by Raabe and Lücke [57]: There is a formation of a strong, incomplete α-fibre and an increase of the intensities along the γ-fibre. However, the intensities along the α-fibre are much higher than those along the γ-fibre.

Furthermore, the results of the rolling induced evolution of the texture can successfully be interpreted and understood on the basis of Taylor type models, among which a distinction can be made between fully constraint [58] and relaxed constraint models [59]. In the former model, each grain is assumed to be exposed to the same strain as the whole sample; in the latter model, it is suggested that shear strains parallel to the rolling plane may also occur. Among the relaxed constraint Taylor type models the C-model (shear strain in the rolling direction is assumed) and the SC-model (shear strain in the rolling and in the transversal direction is assumed) can be distinguished. In particular the SC-model, also referred to as “pancake model”, is often associated with heavily rolled sheets.

In the fully constraint model there are five, in the C-model there are four, and in the SC-model there are only three independent slip systems needed. These independent slip systems can be picked out from the 12 crystallographically equivalent {110} < 111> slip systems or from all 48 slip systems on all {110}, the effective {112}, and the effective {123} planes with Burgers vector of a 0/2〈111〉 (Remark: we assume that the kink-pair nucleation occurs on {110} planes only. Slip along high-indexed planes such as {112}, which is often observed in experiments, is obtained by the glide of the dislocation on two or more {110} planes [15,60]).

Based on comparison of the α-fibre distribution from Fig. 5 with results obtained from texture simulations reported by Raabe and Lücke [57] we conclude that the simulated SC-model with three independent slip systems out of 48 slip systems corresponds well to the experimentally determined rolling textures. From this we infer that only three independent slip systems are active during rolling of the most heavily cold rolled tungsten sheets. Furthermore, we infer that there is slip on the {110} planes as well as on the effective {112} and the effective {123} planes.
The main results of the texture analyses are summarised in Table 3 .

So the BDT temperatures lie in a temperature interval of only 100 K. This shows that the BDT temperature is indeed anisotropic but that the impact of crystallographic texture on the BDT temperature is weak. From this we infer that the dominant contribution of the rolling induced decrease of the BDT temperature from 600 °C down to −65 °C must be traced back to other microstructural features (Fig. 6 ).

The five tungsten sheets assessed within this paper show high intensities for the {001} < 110> texture component. Furthermore, the toughness test samples represent a L-T crack system. By combining both pieces of information, it can be concluded that the five tungsten sheets can be best described as and compared with a {110} < 001> cleavage system. For this system, a transition temperature of 430 K (157 °C) (single crystalline tungsten, loading rate of 0.10 ± 0.02 MPa(m)0.5 1/s, three point bending tests, single edge cracked pure bending specimen (SEB), pre-crack introduced by the bending technique, samples loaded in mode I, [61]) was reported. Our results show a transition temperature of −65 °C (heavily cold rolled tungsten (W4.1LTR), loading rate of 1 ± 0.1 MPa(m)0.5 1/s, single edge cracked tension specimen (SECT), crack introduced by spark erosion, samples loaded in mode I, [40]). Again, this difference in transition temperature confirms that microstructural features beside crystallographic texture have a high impact on the transition temperature. One of these features is grain size, which will be analysed next.

This section is divided into three parts: First, the rolling induced evolution of grain sizes in the ND, TD and the RD is shown. These results allow the calculation of aspect ratios. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the experimentally determined grain size distribution of all the five tungsten sheets investigated in this study can be analytically described by a log-normal distribution.
In the second part, the focus is on the rolling induced evolution of the relative and absolute amount of low and high angle grain boundaries.

Finally, in the third part, a correlation between relevant grain sizes and the BDT temperature is shown. As the fracture toughness test samples represent a L-T crack system, grain size in the ND is a measure for the dislocation source spacing, λ, along the crack front (assumption: the intersection point of grain boundaries with the crack front are preferred dislocation nucleation sites. See Fig. 1b), and grain size in the TD correlates with the mean free path for dislocation glide (relevant of pile up).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Grain size, aspect ratio and grain size distribution
ce:section.ce:para: A first subjective impression of the evolution of the microstructure can be gained from Fig. 7 , in which combined inverse pole figure (IPF) and grain boundary maps of the least rolled and the most heavily rolled tungsten sheets are shown. Fig. 7 provides a view in the RD, TD and the ND (from the left to the right) and the colours in the maps represent the crystallographic directions along the RD.
At first glance it can be anticipated that there is a strong refinement of the microstructure and that the grain shape evolves into a pronounced pancake-like geometry.

Astonishingly, the IPF maps with view in the ND are to some extent untypically for rolled microstructures, as a clear and unambiguous manifestation of pancake shaped grains is missing. This observation can be rationalised by considering the following three facts: the grains are very thin in the ND, the grains are not totally in parallel with the surface of the tungsten sheets, and the grains are expected to be curled and wavy [62].

In order to confirm the pancake-like character of the grains, a 3D-EBSD analysis of a heavily cold rolled tungsten sheet has been performed, and the result can be found in Supplementary Videos 1 and 2. Furthermore, the IPF maps of all five tungsten sheets assessed within this contribution can be found in Supplementary Fig. 3. From the discussion above it can be concluded that the followed-up measurements of grain sizes in the RD and TD underestimate the real grain size.

Furthermore, the IPF maps of all five tungsten sheets assessed within this contribution can be found in Supplementary Fig. 3. From the discussion above it can be concluded that the followed-up measurements of grain sizes in the RD and TD underestimate the real grain size.

Fig. 8a displays the results of the measurement of mean grain size in (or chord length along) the ND, TD and the RD. For the measurement of mean grain size in the ND, a scan representing a view in the TD was used, while for the measurement of mean grain size in the TD and RD, a scan representing a view in the ND was used. The main outcome is that there is a reduction in grain size for all three directions. Note that the rolling was performed unidirectionally for all the tungsten sheets. This result is a clear indication of grain fragmentation during cold rolling. The absolute values of the grain size measurement are summarised in Table 4 .

Furthermore, the grain size data can be used to calculate the rolling induced evolution of the grain aspect ratio. In Fig. 8b the ratio of the mean grain size in the RD to the mean grain size in the ND as well as the ratio of the mean grain size in the TD to the mean grain size in the ND is plotted. The least deformed tungsten sheet (W1.8CR) possesses aspect ratios of 3.56 and 4.82 (TD/ND and RD/ND), and the most heavily cold rolled sheet (W4.1LTR) of 6.87 and 13.73 (TD/ND and RD/ND). The aspect ratio data allow the drawing of conclusions on the grains' shape: the grains are pancake-like.

This section is organised in parallel to the previous one: first a qualitative description and afterwards a quantitative description of grain boundary related issues will be given.

Fig. 10 displays grain boundary maps of the least and the most heavily cold rolled tungsten sheets. Low angle grain boundaries are defined as disorientations between 2° and 15° and are highlighted in grey. High angle grain boundaries are defined as disorientations >15° and are highlighted in black. From Fig. 10 it can be anticipated that heavily cold rolling results in a microstructure which is dominated by high angle grain boundaries. This subjective impression is confirmed by a quantitative description of the microstructure which can be seen in Fig. 11a and b.

In Fig. 11a and b, the number of all pixel pairs with a certain property, divided by the number of all indexed pixels in the EBSD map (= relative number of grain boundaries), is plotted against the degree of deformation and the disorientation angle.

The rolling induced evolution of low and high angle grain boundaries can be traced back to three fundamental processes that work in parallel. Their individual contribution to the rolling induced evolution of the grain size is a function of the applied equivalent strain.

The first fundamental process can be rationalised by pure geometrical consideration: the grain size decreases in the same ratio as the thickness of the rolled plate (process I). In addition to this process, and in particular in cold rolled sheets, a refinement of the grains by grain fragmentation takes place (process II). This process is associated with early and medium stages of rolling. As a result, grain size decreases faster compared to the thickness of the rolled sheets. Finally, there is a third process, described as migration of boundaries during rolling (process III). This process is suggested to play an important role in late stages of rolling. As a result of the migration of the deformed structure, the rolling induced decrease in grain size is smaller than the decrease in the thickness of the rolled sheets.
A phenomenological description of the above mentioned processes as a function of the applied equivalent strain can be found by Sevillano et al. [63].

Fig. 11a displays the rolling induced evolution of grain boundary density. Grain boundary density is defined as the length of the lines representing a certain boundary (e.g high angle grain boundary) divided by the area of the EBSD map. Fig. 11a distinguished between low and high angle grain boundaries. It can be seen that during rolling the grain boundary density of high angle grain boundaries increases while the density of low angle grain boundaries stays constant. This result can be traced back to the aforementioned processes I and II.

Furthermore, the high angle grain boundaries can be subdivided into unspecified high angle grain boundaries and coincident site lattice (CSL) boundaries. The cumulated number fraction of Σ3 to Σ25 coincident site lattice boundaries are also displayed in Fig. 11a. Coincident site lattice boundaries are associated with high strength and low impurity densities [64,65]. Fig. 11a shows that coincident site lattice boundaries are only of minor importance in the microstructures of the five tungsten sheets assessed within this paper. Their density is in the range of about 10% which can be associated with a randomly textured polycrystal [66]. The density of coincident site lattice boundaries does not change significantly during rolling. So the impact of coincident site lattice boundaries on the BDT temperature can be neglected.

Further insights into the rolling induced evolution of low and high angle grain boundaries can be gained from Fig. 11b, in which grain boundary density is plotted against the disorientation angle. Again, it can be seen that cold rolling increases the density of high angle grain boundaries. Furthermore, the five disorientation curves have in common that they possess two peaks. One peak can be found at 54.7°. This peak can successfully be interpreted on the basis of crystallographic texture as the disorientation between the rotated cube component, {001} < 110>, and the components of the γ-fibre, {111} < 110>, {111} < 112>, form an angle of 54.7°. A second peak is at a disorientation of about 7°. This peak can originate from the as-deformed microstructure (grain fragmentation processes) and from the formation of specific crystallographic textures.

More insights into the peak formation at a disorientation at about 7° can be gained from Fig. 11c in which the number fraction (defined as number of pixel pairs with a certain property divided by all indexed pixel pairs with a disorientation angle between 2° and 65°) is plotted against the disorientation angle. In this diagram, the disorientation distributions of the five tungsten sheets are compared with the Mackenzie disorientation distribution. The Mackenzie distribution describes the disorientation distribution for a cubic sample with a random texture. Two results can be drawn from Fig. 11c. First, the heavily cold rolled sheets possess a plateau which is a typical feature of heavily rolled and textured bcc metals. Second, the disorientation distributions of the five tungsten sheets do not follow the Mackenzie distribution. In particular in the disorientation region <15°, the disorientation distributions of the five tungsten sheets possess higher values compared with the Mackenzie distribution. From this we infer that the peak at a disorientation of about 7° from Fig. 11b can to some extent be traced back to the formation of specific crystallographic textures.
In summary, cold rolling decreases the grain size in the ND, TD and the RD, and cold rolling results in microstructures that are dominated by high angle grain boundaries.
The quantitative measures obtained in this section can be used for a microstructure-property-correlation, which will be shown next.

Point “1” belongs to the tungsten sheet that underwent a degree of cold rolling of 3.4, while point “2” belongs to the tungsten sheet that underwent a degree of cold rolling of 3.4 plus an additional degree of deformation of 0.7 after preheating at a temperature < 300 °C (3.4 + 0.7 = 4.1). This severe decrease of the BDT temperature by >120 K, accompanied by only a marginal decrease of the mean grain size in the ND clearly demonstrates that it is not enough to consider only grain sizes. Moreover, additional microstructural features such as dislocation density have to be taken into account in order to arrive at a complete microstructural description of mechanisms controlling crack tip plasticity in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline bcc metals. So the rolling induced evolution of the dislocation density will be determined next.
The dislocation density, ρ, has been determined based on XRD measurements and by evaluating line profiles by the modified Williamson-Hall method.
The results of the measurements are summarised in Table 6 and plotted in Fig. 13a, in which the dislocation density is plotted against the degree of deformation.

The following main conclusions can be drawn: The dislocation density of the cold rolled sheets (W1.8CR – W3.4CR) is in a first approximation constant. The value of the disloation density of these sheets is approximately 1*1014 m−2 which is a typical value for heavily cold rolled materials and fits well to data reported in the literature (1014 to 1015 m−2 [43]). Furthermore, the tungsten sheet that underwent a degree of cold rolling of 3.4 plus and additional degree of deformation of 0.7 after preheating at a temperature < 300 °C (W4.1LTR) possesses a significantly higher dislocation density compared with the density of the cold rolled sheets. For the W3.4CR sheet the dislocation density is 0.92*1014 m−2, while for the W4.1LTR plate the measured dislocation density is 8.8*1014 m−2.

The experimental data allow the correlation between microstructure and BDT temperature. In Fig. 13b the BDT temperature, mean grain size in the ND and the dislocation density (modified Williamson-Hall) are plotted against the degree of deformation. This plot allows the further concretisation of the conclusion drawn in the previous section.

Let us focus on the four cold rolled plates first (W1.8CR – W3.4CR). The dislocation density of these sheets is more or less constant. So the four cold rolled tungsten sheets are microstructures that allow the assessment of impact of the parameter “grain size” in isolation.

In the previous section, we discussed the Hall-Petch-like relation between the BDT temperature and the mean grain size in the ND. With the additional information of the rolling induced evolution of the dislocation density we can conclude the following:

With increasing degree of deformation, both the BDT temperature and the mean grain size in the ND decrease. As the dislocation density stays constant, the decrease of the BDT temperature can be traced back to the impact of the mean grain size in the ND only.

Let us now put the focus on two specific data points which are marked by “1” and “2” in Fig. 13b. Point “1” belongs to the tungsten sheet that underwent a degree of cold rolling of 3.4 (W3.4CR), point “2” belongs to the tungsten sheet that underwent a degree of cold rolling of 3.4 plus an additional degree of deformation of 0.7 after preheating at a temperature < 300 °C (W4.1LTR).

It can be seen in Fig. 13b that the mean grain size in the ND does not change significantly from W3.4CR to W4.1LTR. So W3.4CR and W4.1LTR are microstructures that allow the assessment of the impact of the parameter “dislocation density” in isolation.

During the low-temperature rolling process, dislocation density increases from 0.92*1014 m−2 (W3.4CR) to 8.8*1014 m−2 (W4.1LTR). This increase is accompanied by a severe decrease of the BDT temperature form 60 °C ± 15 °C for the W3.4CR sheet, down to −65 °C ± 15 °C for the W4.1LTR plate. From this we infer that the decrease of the BDT temperature is closely linked with the increase of the dislocation density.

In this work, we consider planar lattice defects (grain boundaries) and line defects (dislocations) only. The rolling induced evolution of point defects such as vacancies or interstitials is not assessed. However, we suggest that their impact on the rolling induced evolution of the BDT temperature is of minor importance.
The results obtained in this “Results” section will now be used for a profound verification and an in-depth discussion of our working hypothesis.

The aim of this section is to elucidate the mechanisms controlling the brittle-to-ductile transition in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline bcc metals. In the Introduction section we introduced our working hypothesis that states that:
1.
The BDT in polycrystalline tungsten is controlled by the glide of screw dislocations, i.e. by the kink-pair nucleation process. So the slowest process in the crack tip region is the glide of screw dislocations.
2.
The temperature at which the transition occurs decreases with decreasing spacing, λ, of dislocation sources along the crack front. Sources for dislocations may be
a.
the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front or
b.
multiplication processes such as e.g. the expansion of open and closed loops, the double cross-slip mechanism [41], the triple junction mechanism [42] or others [43–45].

This section is divided into four parts in which we discuss points 1, 2a and 2b of our working hypothesis and make some comments on the λ-dependence of the BDT temperature. Our working hypothesis contains a further point, referred to as point 3, which says that the aforementioned processes are overlapped by the geometrical arrangement of areas with high and low fracture toughness (e.g. former sinter pore) with respect to the crack system. This last point describes the anisotropy of the rolling induced evolution of the BDT temperature and is not assessed within this study.
To confirm point 1 of our working hypothesis, we correlate the toughness values at and above the BDT temperature with the yield stress of the tungsten sheets.
Finally, point 2a and 2b elucidates the contradictory role of long-range obstacles such as grain boundaries and forest dislocations on the BDT temperature.

The impact of long-range obstacles on strength is straightforward and well described by the grain boundary and dislocation hardening models. The mechanisms of these models can be traced back to a reduced dislocation mobility caused by obstacles. However, the question of the role of long-range obstacles on the BDT has not yet been resolved.

On the one hand, grain boundaries and forest dislocations can act as obstacles for dislocation glide. Based on these considerations, the application of the hardening mechanisms such as grain boundary hardening or dislocation hardening would lead to an increase of the BDT temperature.

On the other hand, grain boundaries and dislocations can act as a dislocation source. For example, the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front are preferred dislocation nucleation sites. Furthermore, pre-existing dislocations can multiply and can thus also be regarded as dislocation sources.

It can be expected that both mechanisms viz. being an obstacle for dislocation glide and being a preferred site for dislocation nucleation, apply for long range obstacles. In this section, we will show how to weight the single contributions.

ce:section.ce:section-title: To our working hypothesis, point 1: The BDT in polycrystalline tungsten is controlled by the glide of screw dislocations
ce:section.ce:para: Crack tip plasticity can be described as the net result of the following sequential processes: (i) the nucleation of fresh dislocations from sources, (ii) their glide through the crystal, and (iii) their interaction with long-range obstacles such as the pile up at grain boundaries. It can be anticipated that the slowest of these processes is rate controlling and thus controls the BDT.
Here we demonstrate that the slowest crack tip plasticity process is the glide of screw dislocations or more precisely their kink-pair nucleation process.

Our approach looks as follows: We assess whether it is possible to scale the toughness data at and above the BDT temperature with the yield stress, σ

ce:section.ce:section-title: To our working hypothesis, point 2 a: On the contradictory role of grain boundaries – dislocation nucleation sites vs. obstacles for dislocation glide (pile up)
ce:section.ce:para: In this section we focus on grain boundaries. In the first part we recall and reflect on the correlation between microstructure and BDT temperature and arrive at a confirmation of our working hypothesis. Afterwards, we give some quantitative measures for the obstacle forces provided by grain boundaries. Finally, we compare the dislocation source spacing, λ, of single crystalline and polycrystalline tungsten.

ce:section.ce:section-title: The verification of the working hypothesis
ce:section.ce:para: In section “3.3. Dislocation density” we showed that the dislocation density of the cold rolled sheets W1.8CR, W2.5CR, W3.0CR and W3.4CR is in a first approximation constant. This makes these four plates ideal microstructures for the assessment of the impact of grain size on the BDT temperature, as the grain size, d, is the only material variable.

In section “3.2. Grain size” we have shown that during cold rolling the grain size decreases in all three main directions, the ND, TD and the RD. Furthermore, we have shown that for samples with a L-T crack system, the grain size in the ND is a measure for the dislocation source spacing, λ, along the crack front and that the grain size in the TD scales with the mean free path for dislocation glide.

We finally arrive at the following conclusion: our experimental results show that the BDT temperature decreases with decreasing grain size. From this we infer, that the positive impact of grain boundaries on the BDT temperature outperforms the negative. In addition, we proposed an analytical relation between the BDT temperature and the mean grain size in the ND. From this we conclude, that the temperature at which the transition occurs decreases with decreasing spacing, λ, of dislocation sources along the crack front and that sources for dislocations are the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparison of the dislocation source spacing in singlecrystalline and polycrystalline tungsten
ce:section.ce:para: The spacing, λ, of the nucleation sites in tungsten single crystals can be derived from experimental observations. Riedle [61] assessed the fractured surfaces of {100} < 010> cracks produced at 77 K and 298 K. The surfaces were etched to make traces of dislocation activity visible. From these surfaces the source spacing was estimated to be λ 1 = 60 μm at T 1 = 77 K and λ 2 = 3 μm at T 2 = 298 K.

In polycrystalline tungsten, our experimental results suggest that the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front are preferred dislocation nucleation sites viz. the mean grain sizes in the ND is a measure for the dislocation source spacing.

In general, the impact of grain boundaries on toughness and the BDT temperature can be summarised as follows: the BDT temperature decreases by grain refinement. The positive impact of grain boundaries (sources for dislocations) on toughness and the BDT temperature outperforms the negative (obstacles for dislocation glide).
In the next section we will discuss how another type of long-range obstacle i.e. forest dislocations, impacts on toughness and the BDT temperature.

ce:section.ce:section-title: To our working hypothesis, point 2 b: critical dislocation density for multiplication processes
ce:section.ce:para: Dislocations can be both: (i) obstacles for gliding dislocations and (ii) sources for fresh dislocations. Here we want to demonstrate that the positive impact of dislocations outperforms the negative and thus confirm our working hypothesis that states that the temperature at which the transition occurs decreases with decreasing spacing, λ, of dislocation sources along the crack front and that sources for dislocations may be dislocation multiplication processes.

We put the focus on two specific tungsten sheets. The first one is the plate that was deformed with a degree of cold rolling of 3.4 (W3.4CR), the second one is the tungsten sheet that was deformed with a degree of cold rolling of 3.4 plus and additional degree of deformation of 0.7 after preheating at a temperature < 300 °C (W4.1LTR).

In section “3.2. Grain size” we showed that for W3.4CR and W4.1LTR the mean grain size in the ND is almost constant. This makes these two plates ideal microstructures for the assessment of the impact of dislocation density on the BDT temperature, as dislocation density, ρ, is the only material variable.

In Fig. 16 the BDT temperature and the dislocation density are plotted against the degree of deformation. It can be seen that an increase in dislocation density severely decreases the BDT temperature. We suggest that the decrease in the BDT temperature can again be traced back to a decrease of the dislocation source spacing. However, in this case the sources for dislocations are dislocation multiplication processes.

Among the multiplication processes it can be distinguished between stable sources (regenerative multiplication of dislocations) that emit a large number of loops and temporary ones operating during dislocation motion (cross slip or the expansion of open and closed loops) [44]. A summary of possible multiplication processes can be found in Anderson et al. [50], Hull and Bacon [43] and Caillard and Martin [44].

Assessment of the heavily cold rolled tungsten sheets by transmission electron microscopy revealed particular dislocation features [72]. These are junctions, bulges, dislocation loops and prismatic loops. The latter are often observed features in heavily deformed materials. This so called debris is left behind by moving dislocations and is a direct result of edge jogs on a screw [43]. Based on these dislocation features, it can be speculated that the triple junction mechanism [42] or the double cross slip mechanism ([41], also referred to as multiple cross glide source [43]), may occur and operate in the crack tip region (both are regenerative multiplication processes).

Furthermore, we suggest that the onset of temporary dislocation multiplication processes require a certain, critical dislocation density. More precisely, we assume that there is a critical dislocation density (viz. a critical distance between neighbouring dislocations, L

This change in the relative length scale is required to approach a bulk like multiplication behaviour of dislocations within a grain. From this we infer that for low dislocation densities, crack tip plasticity is governed by dislocation nucleation processes (e.g. dislocations are nucleated at the intersection points of grain boundaries and the crack front). In contrast, for materials with high dislocation densities, crack tip plasticity is governed by dislocation multiplication processes. Further details on the change from nucleation controlled plasticity towards multiplication controlled plasticity can be found by El-Awady [73].
Ongoing work, in particular modelling by means of discrete dislocation dynamics, may help to answer open questions about dislocation nucleation and multiplication in the crack tip region.
One mayor result of this work is the identification of the λ-dependence of the BDT temperature. In the next section, this issue will be discussed in light of crack tip plasticity processes.

The comparison of microstructural features with experimental results revealed that the dislocation source spacing, λ, is one of the most important parameter in crack tip plasticity, as the BDT temperature, T
BDT , is a function of λ, viz. T
BDT = f(λ).

Here we discuss the λ-dependence of the BDT temperature with the help of K
eff -over-K
app -plots. K
app is the global, externally applied load, K
eff is the local, effective stress intensity at the crack tip (see Fig. 1a). The effective stress intensity at the crack tip differs from the applied load, as the elastic stress fields from dislocations impact on K
eff , leading to a lower K
eff compared to K
app due to shielding effects by dislocations. Furthermore, the Griffith critical stress intensity, K
IC , is the critical parameter for fracture.

In Fig. 17 , a schematic plot of K
eff versus K
app is shown. This schematic representation diagram shows a horizontal line which gives the criterion for fracture viz. K
eff = K
IC . The material behaviour can be classified as brittle, if K
eff reaches the critical stress intensity. The material behaviour can be classified as ductile, if K
eff never reaches the critical stress intensity for any applied load. In the latter case the curve shows asymptotic behaviour for high values of K
app . Fig. 17 will now be used to provide an explanation of the λ-dependence of the BDT temperature.

Three case studies are shown: The first one describes brittle material behaviour and is related to a low test temperature, the second one describes the transition from brittle to ductile material behaviour and is related to an intermediate test temperature, and finally case study three describes ductile material behaviour and is related to a high test temperature. In each of these case studies, the impact of dislocation source spacing, λ, on the shape of the K
eff -K
app -curve is shown.

It can be seen that at low test temperatures (case study one), the criterion for brittle behaviour is reached. This is true both for the curve representing a high value of λ, and for the curve representing a low value for λ. However, it can be seen that the applied load at which the fracture criterion is reached increases with decreased dislocation source spacing.

Furthermore, it can be seen from Fig. 17 that at high test temperatures (case study three), the criterion for brittle behaviour is never reached for any external applied load. The material behaviour is ductile. This is true both for the curve representing a high value of λ, and for the curve representing a low value for λ.

The most interesting case study is case study two, representing the material behaviour at intermediate temperatures. It can be seen that for a high value of the dislocations source spacing, the criterion for brittle fracture is reached. However, for a low value of the dislocations source spacing the K
eff -K
app -curve shows asymptotic behaviour at high applied loads and the criterion for brittle fracture is never reached for any applied load. The material behaviour can thus be classified as ductile. This example shows how the dislocation source spacing impacts on the BDT temperature.

In this work, we arrived at a rough but complete microstructural description of mechanisms controlling crack tip plasticity in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline bcc metals. Ongoing work, in particular the modelling of crack tip plasticity by means of discrete dislocation dynamics, should confirm our working hypotheses and provide more insight into dislocation nucleation and dislocation multiplication processes in the crack tip region.

The aim of this paper was to elucidate the mechanisms controlling the brittle-to-ductile transition in pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline bcc metals by the example of cold rolled tungsten. For this purpose, five tungsten sheets were rolled out from one and the same sintered ingot, by various levels, representing degrees of deformation of 1.8, 2.5, 3.0, 3.4, and 4.1.

Toughness tests show that the BDT temperature decreases with increasing degree of deformation from 115 °C ± 15 °C (388 K ± 15 K) down to −65 °C ± 15 °C (208 K ± 15 K). In this paper we performed an in-depth analysis of the microstructure of the five sheets mentioned above. This analysis included the assessment of (i) crystallographic texture, (ii) grain size and (iii) dislocation density.

Our results show that the cold rolled sheets W1.8CR, W2.5CR, W3.0CR and W3.4CR, possess more or less the same dislocation density, ρ, and thus the grain size, d, is the only material variable. This makes these sheets ideal materials for the assessment of the impact of grain size on the BDT temperature.

Furthermore, we have shown that the grain size, d, of the sheets W3.4CR and W4.1LTR is almost the same and the dislocation density, ρ, is the only material variable. This makes these two sheets ideal microstructures to assess the impact of dislocation density on the BDT temperature.

Coming back to the main questions posed in the “Introduction” section we can now, by the end of this paper, conclude the following:
1.
What is the impact of crystallographic texture, grain size and dislocations density on the BDT temperature?

Our results show that the impact of crystallographic texture on the BDT temperature is weak. Furthermore, we were able to demonstrate that the BDT temperature is a function of grain size following a Hall-Petch-like relation. In addition, we showed that an increase of the dislocation density decreases the BDT temperature.
2.
Is it possible to resolve the question on the contradictory role of long-range obstacles on the BDT temperature (obstacles for dislocations glide vs. sources for dislocations)?

A correlation between microstructural features and experimental data allowed the discussion on the contradictory role of long-range obstacles on the BDT temperature. On the one hand, grain boundaries and forest dislocations can act as obstacles for dislocation glide. On the other hand, grain boundaries and dislocations can act as a dislocation source. Our results clearly show that the positive impact of long-range obstacles outperforms the negative.
3.
How can a correlation between experimental data and microstructural features give indications towards a change from nucleation controlled to multiplication controlled crack tip plasticity? And: To what extent can our working hypothesis be verified or falsified?

In this paper we verified our working hypothesis which states that the BDT is controlled by the glide of screw dislocations and that the transition temperature decreases with decreasing spacing, λ, of dislocation sources along the crack front. Sources for dislocations may be the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front (BDT-temperature-grain-size-relation, nucleation controlled plasticity) or dislocation multiplication processes such as e.g., the expansion of open and closed loops (impact of dislocation density on the BDT temperature, multiplication controlled plasticity).

Ongoing work should elucidate whether our findings can also be applied to other bcc metals that differ in cross-slip behaviour, non-Schmid behaviour, elastic anisotropy, electron configuration and fabrication type (sintered vs. conventional melted and casted materials). In addition, ongoing investigations should identify whether our results derived from the assessment of the transition metal tungsten are also true for predominantly covalently bonded materials such as intermetallics (e.g nickel-aluminium) or ceramics (e.g. alumina).
